title: UNIT 2: POLYNOMIAL FUNCTIONS
notes:
✓ Polynomial function → a function of the form :- 

p(x) = aₙxⁿ + aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹ + ... + a₂x² + a₁x + a₀, where n is a non-negative integer and aₙ ≠ 0.

title: POLYNOMIAL EXPRESSION
notes:
✓ Polynomial expression → an expression of the form:
aₙxⁿ + aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹ + ... + a₁x + a₀

◆ Term → each individual part aₖxᵏ.

◆ Coefficient → numerical factor multiplying a variable.

◆ Constant term → term without a variable.

◆ Degree → highest exponent of x with a non-zero coefficient.

◆ Leading coefficient → coefficient of the highest-degree term.

Example:
p(x)=3x⁵−2x³+7x−4
Degree = 5
Leading coefficient = 3
Constant term = −4.

title: WHAT IS NOT A POLYNOMIAL?
notes:
✓ An expression is not a polynomial in x if the variable has a negative or non-integer exponent, appears in a denominator, or occurs inside a radical.

Examples:
◆ 1/x² → not a polynomial.
◆ √x → not a polynomial.
◆ x⁻³ → not a polynomial.

3x⁴−2x²+x+5 → polynomial.

✓ Powers of x in a polynomial must be non-negative integers.

title: TYPES OF POLYNOMIAL FUNCTIONS
notes:
◆ Constant function:
f(x)=b
Degree = 0.

◆ Linear function:
f(x)=ax+b, a≠0
Degree = 1.

◆ Quadratic function:
f(x)=ax²+bx+c, a≠0
Degree = 2.

◆ Cubic function:
f(x)=ax³+bx²+cx+d, a≠0
Degree = 3.

Higher-degree polynomials have degree 4, 5, 6, ... depending on their highest power.

title: POLYNOMIALS OVER DIFFERENT NUMBER SYSTEMS
notes:
◆ Polynomial over integers → all coefficients are integers.

◆ Polynomial over rational numbers → all coefficients are rational numbers.

◆ Polynomial over real numbers → all coefficients are real numbers.

Example:
p(x)=2x³−5x+1
has integer, rational and real coefficients.

✓ The type depends on the number system containing the coefficients.

title: 2.2 OPERATIONS ON POLYNOMIAL FUNCTIONS
notes:
✓ Polynomial functions can be combined using the four fundamental operations:

◆ Addition:
(f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x)

◆ Subtraction:
(f−g)(x)=f(x)−g(x)

◆ Multiplication:
(fg)(x)=f(x)g(x)

◆ Division:
(f÷g)(x)=f(x)÷g(x), where g(x)≠0.

✓ Like terms are combined when adding or subtracting polynomials.

title: ADDITION & SUBTRACTION OF POLYNOMIALS
notes:
✓ To add or subtract polynomials, combine like terms.

Example:
f(x)=2x³+3x²−x+4
g(x)=x³−2x²+5x−1

(f+g)(x)=3x³+x²+4x+3.

(f−g)(x)=x³+5x²−6x+5.

✓ Like terms have the same variable and the same exponent.

title: MULTIPLICATION OF POLYNOMIALS
notes:
✓ Use the distributive property to multiply every term in one polynomial by every term in the other.

Example:
(x+2)(x+3)
= x²+3x+2x+6
= x²+5x+6.

Important laws:
a(b+c)=ab+ac

✓ After multiplying, combine like terms.

title: DIVISION OF POLYNOMIALS
notes:
✓ Polynomial division is similar to ordinary long division.

When dividing f(x) by g(x), obtain:
Dividend = Divisor × Quotient + Remainder.

✓ Stop when the degree of the remainder is less than the degree of the divisor.

Example:
x³−1 divided by x−1 gives:
x³−1=(x−1)(x²+x+1)+0.

Therefore the quotient is x²+x+1 and the remainder is 0.

title: 2.3 POLYNOMIAL DIVISION THEOREM
notes:
✓ If f(x) and d(x) are polynomials, d(x)≠0, and degree of d(x) ≤ degree of f(x), then there are unique polynomials q(x) and r(x) such that:

f(x)=d(x)q(x)+r(x)

where:
r(x)=0 or degree of r(x) < degree of d(x).

This is the Polynomial Division Theorem.

title: REMAINDER THEOREM
notes:
✓ Remainder Theorem → when a polynomial f(x) is divided by x−c, the remainder is f(c).

✓ Formula:
Remainder = f(c)

Example:
f(x)=x²+2x+3
Divide by x−2.

Remainder = f(2)
=4+4+3
=11.

Therefore the remainder is 11.

title: FACTOR THEOREM
notes:
✓ Factor Theorem → x−c is a factor of f(x) if and only if f(c)=0.

✓ Rule:
f(c)=0 ⇔ x−c is a factor of f(x).

Example:
f(x)=x²−5x+6

f(2)=4−10+6=0.

Therefore x−2 is a factor.

Factoring:
x²−5x+6=(x−2)(x−3).

title: 2.4 ZEROS OF A POLYNOMIAL
notes:
✓ Zero of a polynomial → a value c for which:
f(c)=0.

The zeros are also called roots or solutions of f(x)=0.

✓ Relationship:
Zero c ⇔ x−c is a factor.

Example:
f(x)=(x−2)(x+3)

Zeros:
x=2 and x=−3.

The corresponding x-intercepts are (2,0) and (−3,0).

title: RATIONAL & IRRATIONAL ZEROS
notes:
✓ Rational zero → a zero that can be written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q≠0.

✓ Irrational zero → a real zero that cannot be expressed as a ratio of integers.

Example:
f(x)=x²−3

Zeros:
x=±√3.

Since √3 is irrational, both zeros are irrational.

Polynomial zeros may be rational, irrational, or non-real.

title: RATIONAL ZERO TEST
notes:
✓ For a polynomial with integer coefficients:
p(x)=aₙxⁿ+...+a₀

Possible rational zeros have the form:
±p/q

◆ p → factor of the constant term a₀.
◆ q → factor of the leading coefficient aₙ.

Example:
p(x)=2x³+3x²−8x−12

Possible rational zeros are obtained from factors of 12 divided by factors of 2.

The test gives possible candidates; each candidate must be checked.

title: LOCATION THEOREM
notes:
✓ Location Theorem → if f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, then a polynomial f has at least one zero between a and b.

✓ Condition:
f(a)·f(b)<0

Example:
f(1)>0 and f(2)<0.

Therefore f has at least one zero between 1 and 2.

This theorem is useful for locating real zeros, especially irrational zeros.

title: NUMBER OF POSSIBLE ZEROS
notes:
✓ A polynomial of degree n can have at most n real zeros.

Example:
A cubic polynomial has degree 3, so it can have at most 3 real zeros.

A fourth-degree polynomial can have at most 4 real zeros.

The number of real zeros may be less than the degree because some zeros may be repeated or non-real.

title: MULTIPLICITY OF A ZERO
notes:
✓ Multiplicity → the number of times a factor corresponding to a zero occurs.

Example:
f(x)=(x−2)³(x+1)

Zero x=2 has multiplicity 3.
Zero x=−1 has multiplicity 1.

◆ Even multiplicity → graph generally touches the x-axis and turns back.
◆ Odd multiplicity → graph generally crosses the x-axis.

Multiplicity helps describe the behavior of polynomial graphs at their zeros.

title: 2.5 GRAPHS OF POLYNOMIAL FUNCTIONS
notes:
✓ The graph of a polynomial is the set of points (x,f(x)).

◆ Important features include:
• x-intercepts
• y-intercept
• Zeros
• Turning points
• Degree
• Leading coefficient
• End behavior
• Multiplicity

y-intercept → f(0).
x-intercepts → values where f(x)=0.

title: X-INTERCEPT & Y-INTERCEPT
notes:
✓ x-intercept → where the graph crosses or touches the x-axis.

To find it:
f(x)=0.

y-intercept → where the graph crosses the y-axis.

To find it:
x=0.

Example:
f(x)=x²−4x+3

x-intercepts:
(x−1)(x−3)=0
x=1,3.

y-intercept:
f(0)=3 → (0,3).

title: END BEHAVIOR OF POLYNOMIALS
notes:
✓ End behavior describes what happens to f(x) as x becomes very large positive or negative.

◆ Even degree + positive leading coefficient → both ends go upward.

◆ Even degree + negative leading coefficient → both ends go downward.

◆ Odd degree + positive leading coefficient → left end down, right end up.

◆ Odd degree + negative leading coefficient → left end up, right end down.

✓ Degree determines the general shape; leading coefficient determines the direction.

title: ODD-DEGREE POLYNOMIALS
notes:
✓ For an odd-degree polynomial:

◆ Positive leading coefficient:
As x→−∞, f(x)→−∞
As x→+∞, f(x)→+∞

◆ Negative leading coefficient:
As x→−∞, f(x)→+∞
As x→+∞, f(x)→−∞

Odd-degree polynomial graphs have opposite end directions.

title: EVEN-DEGREE POLYNOMIALS
notes:
✓ For an even-degree polynomial:

◆ Positive leading coefficient:
Both ends rise upward.

◆ Negative leading coefficient:
Both ends fall downward.

Example:
f(x)=x⁴−2x²+1
→ degree 4, positive leading coefficient.
→ both ends rise.

Example:
g(x)=−x⁴+x²
→ degree 4, negative leading coefficient.
→ both ends fall.

title: TURNING POINTS
notes:
✓ Turning point → a point where the graph changes direction from increasing to decreasing or from decreasing to increasing.

✓ A polynomial of degree n can have at most n−1 turning points.

Examples:
◆ Degree 2 → at most 1 turning point.
◆ Degree 3 → at most 2 turning points.
◆ Degree 4 → at most 3 turning points.

For general higher-degree polynomials, finding exact turning points requires more advanced methods.

title: POLYNOMIAL GRAPH & NUMBER OF X-INTERCEPTS
notes:
✓ A polynomial of degree n can have at most n x-intercepts.

Example:
A fourth-degree polynomial can intersect the x-axis at most 4 times.

It may have fewer intersections.

A fourth-degree polynomial may have:
◆ 0 real x-intercepts
◆ 1 or 2 real x-intercepts
◆ 3 or 4 real x-intercepts, depending on its zeros.

x-intercepts correspond to real zeros.

title: UNIT 2 QUICK FORMULA SUMMARY
notes:
✓ Polynomial:
p(x)=aₙxⁿ+...+a₁x+a₀, aₙ≠0.

✓ Degree → highest exponent.
✓ Leading coefficient → coefficient of highest-degree term.

✓ (f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x)
✓ (f−g)(x)=f(x)−g(x)
✓ (fg)(x)=f(x)g(x)
✓ (f÷g)(x)=f(x)/g(x), g(x)≠0.

✓ Division:
f(x)=d(x)q(x)+r(x)

✓ Remainder theorem:
Remainder when divided by x−c = f(c).

✓ Factor theorem:
x−c is a factor ⇔ f(c)=0.

✓ Zero:
f(c)=0.

✓ Location theorem:
f(a)f(b)<0 → at least one zero between a and b.

✓ Maximum number of real zeros = degree.
✓ Maximum turning points = degree−1.

✓ End behavior depends on degree and leading coefficient.
